opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really exciting moment for hardware, and it's shifting what matters. For the last several years, the story was all about training — who could assemble the biggest cluster, the most tightly interconnected GPUs, to push a single massive pre-training run. That's still important, but as we move toward models that spend more compute at inference time — reasoning, searching, checking their own work — the center of gravity starts to move toward serving.

And inference has a very different profile. You care a lot more about memory bandwidth, latency, cost per token, and energy efficiency than raw peak FLOPs on a giant synchronized job. That opens the door for a much more diverse hardware ecosystem. You've got Nvidia obviously still dominant, but AMD is getting genuinely competitive, the hyperscalers have their own chips, and there's a wave of startups building inference-specialized silicon. When the workload is inference-heavy, some of those specialized architectures start to make a lot more sense economically.

For a company like ours, that's good news. We've always been focused on enterprise, on efficiency, on making models that can actually be deployed — sometimes on-prem, sometimes in a customer's own VPC, on whatever hardware they have. So hardware diversity and falling inference costs directly translate into more of our customers being able to use reasoning models in production without the bill becoming prohibitive.

The other thing I'd say is that test-time compute changes the demand curve. It's not a fixed cost per query anymore — you can choose to think longer on harder problems. That means demand for compute is effectively elastic and probably much larger than people forecast a couple of years ago. So I don't buy the narrative that we're going to have a glut of compute. If anything, as reasoning gets more useful, people will want to spend more of it, and the bottleneck shifts to power, data centers, and supply chain more than to the chips themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says inference can use more compute and its cost varies by problem, but does not state that test-time compute makes inference roughly three to ten times as expensive.

r002.rationale: The response describes a diverse hardware ecosystem, but does not say different chip types can be combined into an effective supercomputer for training models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the shift to test-time compute is a pretty big deal for the hardware story, and it changes the picture in a way that I don't think the market has fully internalized yet.

For the last few years, the narrative was all about training. You build a giant cluster, you run one enormous job for a few months, you get a model out the other end, and then inference was kind of an afterthought. And the hardware that's optimal for that regime is basically what Nvidia built: huge amounts of dense compute, very high bandwidth interconnect, everything tuned for massive matrix multiplies in parallel.

Test-time compute flips the ratio. If the model is now thinking for seconds or minutes per query, running long chains of reasoning, calling tools, checking its own work, then the bulk of the FLOPs in the system move from training to serving. And inference has very different characteristics. It's memory-bandwidth bound more than compute bound, it's latency sensitive, and it's much more amenable to specialized silicon. You don't need the same flexibility you need during training because the workload is more predictable.

So my read is a couple of things. One, total demand for compute goes up, not down. People sometimes hear "smaller models that think longer" and assume that's bearish for chips. I think it's the opposite. You're trading a one-time training cost for a recurring per-query cost, and the per-query cost scales with how much value you're trying to extract. That's a much bigger and more durable market.

Two, the competitive landscape opens up. Training has been very hard to dislodge Nvidia from because of CUDA and the software ecosystem. Inference is a different story. We're already seeing that at Cohere, where we run on a mix of hardware, and the inference-focused players, whether that's the hyperscalers' own chips or the startups building purpose-built inference accelerators, have a real shot because the workload rewards memory bandwidth and efficiency per token more than raw peak throughput.

And three, from an enterprise point of view, which is where we live, this makes the economics of deployment much more tractable. A customer can decide how much compute to spend per task depending on how much the task is worth. A quick lookup gets a fast cheap answer, a complex multi-step analysis gets more thinking time. That dial didn't really exist before, and it makes the cost side of AI feel a lot less like a fixed tax and a lot more like something you can actually manage.

So overall I'm quite bullish. I just think the winners on the hardware side over the next few years might look different from the winners of the last few.

r001.rationale: The response says test-time compute raises recurring inference costs and compute demand, but it does not state that inference becomes roughly three to ten times as expensive.

r002.rationale: The response mentions running inference on a mix of hardware and specialized inference chips, but does not say different chips can be combined into an effective supercomputer for training models.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes the shape of the demand. With training, you’ve got this enormous job running across a tightly connected cluster. With test-time compute, you’re spending more compute as people use the model, so inference becomes a much bigger part of the picture.

And that creates opportunities for different hardware. You care about how cheaply you can generate tokens, but also how quickly, because if the model is going to spend longer working through a problem, the user still needs an answer in a reasonable amount of time. Memory, bandwidth, and utilization all matter, and the best system may depend on how that reasoning is structured.

So I’m optimistic about more diversity in the hardware market. But a chip being good on paper isn’t enough. The software has to make it easy to deploy models and keep up as they change. That’s a huge part of whether a new architecture actually gets adopted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes the hardware picture a lot more interesting. Historically, so much of the focus has been on training: how do you connect a huge number of chips and keep them busy on one enormous run? With test-time compute, you’re spending more computation answering the question, so inference becomes a much bigger part of the equation.

But the workload matters. If you’re generating a long chain of reasoning sequentially, latency and memory bandwidth become really important. If you’re exploring lots of possible answers in parallel, that’s a different workload, and you can use the hardware differently. So I don’t think there’s one obvious hardware consequence of “more test-time compute.” It depends on how we actually build these systems.

The thing I’m optimistic about is that there’s a lot of room to make inference cheaper and more efficient. The question is how much useful work you can get out of each dollar of compute, within the time somebody is willing to wait. That creates a pretty strong incentive for both better chips and better algorithms.
